entries.title: Pope Leo XIV begins four-day pilgrimage to France
entries.summary: The pope has landed in Paris, where he and President Macron will navigate the rules of religious state visits in secular France. Leo's trip will mix pilgrimage and politics on questions of morality and human existence.
entries.content:
France

Pope Leo XIV begins four-day pilgrimage to France

September 25, 2026

The pope has landed in Paris, where he and President Macron will navigate the rules of religious state visits in secular France. Leo's trip will mix pilgrimage and politics on questions of morality and human existence.

Pope Leo XIV arrived for a four-day visit to France on Friday, the first official papal visit to the strictly secular country in 18 years.

Leo, the spiritual leader of the some 1.4 billion Catholics worldwide, was greeted at Paris' Orly Airport by French President Emmanuel Macron and will be in the country until Monday.

The papal itinerary has Leo meeting Macron at the Elysee Palace, speaking at UNESCO headquarters, leading Vespers at Notre Dame Cathedral and celebrating Mass for an estimated 80,000 young people at the Stade de France national stadium on Friday.

On Saturday, he is scheduled to celebrate Mass for another 600,000 at Place de la Concorde on the Avenue des Champs-Elysees before departing for Lourdes, a famous Catholic pilgrimage site located near France's Spanish border.

On Monday, Leo will travel to Metz, near the German border, where he will deliver a speech entitled: "To the roots of Europe for peace and unity." Macron will introduce Leo at the event and has invited fellow leaders across the EU to join him in attendance.

Pope speaks of press freedom on flight to France

While traveling to France, US-born Leo was asked by a CNN reporter for his thoughts on US President Donald Trump's attempts to ban news outlets from covering him.

"I am very happy that here, you are all welcome," he told reporters.

Leo, who was forced to fly home alone after plane trouble on a recent trip to Spain, took the opportunity to apologize to his press pool.

Speaking to reporters at the back of his plane on Friday, Leo said, "I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn't have the flight back together back to Rome."

AI, abuse, peace all on the agenda

Leo is expected to address global concerns regarding so-called artificial intelligence (AI) and the "new dangers" it presents to "security and international peace" during discussions with Macron.

Speaking at the Vatican on Thursday, Leo said leaders must "govern wisely" when dealing with the new technology, which he says raises questions about the very essence of what it means to be human.

The pope is also seeking to repair the Catholic Church's standing in France, where opinions grew particularly bleak in 2021 following the publication of a report documenting seven decades of abuse — impacting 330,000 French children — by clergy and lay leaders.

Leo will meet victims of church abuse during the trip.

Upon arriving in France, Pope Leo, who has been a tireless critic of the wars in Ukraine, Iran and elsewhere, said he sought to be "a pilgrim for peace" in a time of war.

entries.title: Volkswagen, Audi to recall almost 1 million cars in Germany
entries.summary: Volkswagen and its subsidiary Audi are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to a potential steering fault.
entries.content:
September 25, 2026

Volkswagen and its subsidiary Audi are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to a potential steering fault.

Germany auto firm Volkswagen (VW) and its daughter company Audi are to recall nearly a million vehicles in Germany due to steering problems, according to German media reports.

The KBA road traffic authority was cited by the t-online news portal as saying that the recall was required due to potential bolt failures that could damage the steering gearbox or, in some cases, cause a complete loss of steering.

The bolts are to be replaced with ones resistant to corrosion caused by humidity.

Autor Motor Sport magazine reported that VW believed the steering issue would impact only a smaller proportion of the recalled vehicles.

The company said there were no known cases of accidents or injuries caused by the possible bolt failure.

According to KBA, the VW models Tiguan, Touran, Golf Variant, Caddy und Golf produced between September 24, 2013, and July 1, 2024, are impacted by the recall.

This is equivalent to around 900,000 vehicles in Germany and 2.16 million around the world.

For Audi, the model in question is the Q3, with 700,000 vehicles around the world impacted, including 58,555 in Germany.

The recall comes as VW grapples with dwindling sales in recent years, with the firm laying off tens of thousands of staff and shrinking plants in order to cut costs.

entries.title: Why farmers are pairing crops with solar panels
entries.summary: From cooler soil to paid grazing land, farmers are finding solar panels can do more than generate power.
entries.content:
September 25, 2026

From cooler soil to paid grazing land, farmers are finding solar panels can do more than generate power.

Traditionally, solar panel farms are quiet — save for the faint hum of the inverter. But on about one in ten of American solar farms, there's a new sound reverberating through fields: baaaa.

Letting sheep roam under solar panels is just one of many forms of a burgeoning strategy called agrivoltaics, where crops grow or livestock graze in tandem with renewable energy infrastructure.

It's not only of potential benefit for the animals, which get additional shade. The panels can also protect crops from the elements as well as divert water to them, creating cooler, damper conditions that even boost yields.

And even the solar panels themselves tend to respond well to this co-existence — as the cooler they are, the more electricity they produce per watt of sunlight. 

"Having concrete or something underneath the solar panels — you're going to have lower efficiency than having something like plants that are transpiring and cooling off on the land surface," Carl Bernacchi, professor of plant biology and crop sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, told DW.

While the potential is enormous, especially as climate change puts more and more heat stress on agriculture, the practice is still in its infancy. In Europe, if agrivoltaics were implemented on just 1% of available agricultural land, the continent could exceed its solar energy targets for 2030.   

But uptake has been slow: agrivoltaics represents just 18.4 gigawatts of energy worldwide as of mid-2025, less than 1% of the world's solar capacity.  

What thrives under the panels

The idea for agrivoltaics dates back to 1981, when two German scientists published an article titled "Kartoffeln unter dem Kollektor" (or "Potatoes beneath the collector"). But the first pilot project didn't begin until 2004 in Japan, a land-constrained country, where there's particular concern over balancing solar deployment with the protection of farmland.

There are three main types of agrivoltaics: horizontal, where panels look directly up at the sky, vertical, where they're placed in large rows, perpendicular to the ground, and integrated, often installed atop greenhouses.

Research suggests shade-tolerant crops stand to benefit. That includes berries, grapes and tomatoes — where the panels' steel framing often doubles as trellises — as well as peaches and peppers.

The panels can also prevent water from fully evaporating, creating a more humid microclimate that benefits the soil — though humidity is a double-edged sword, sometimes introducing plant disease.

Sheep have also proven to be a particularly good match. Compared to cattle or goats, they're generally easier to manage around solar infrastructure, less likely to damage equipment, and small enough to fit comfortably beneath panels. The practice has other sustainability upsides too: sheep manure fertilizes the soil, and sites require less herbicide.

"If we look at the sheep industry, this has been a real paradigm shift for them, where instead of having to pay to lease land to graze their animals — now they're actually getting paid to graze," Kinzer said. "So it completely puts the economics on its head and is a huge opportunity for the sheep industry, which is really struggling in the US pretty much since World War II."

A double climate win

Agrivoltaics sit at a rare intersection of climate mitigation (cutting emissions) and adaptation (adjusting to a warming planet).

"It is both, which is pretty unique as far as climate solutions go," Kinzer said.

The practice offers one answer to where solar panels could go, helping to produce cheaper and more efficient energy, while also benefiting crops that might struggle due to rising temperatures or volatile weather.

And research suggests that climate change will only make regions grow drier, "broadening areas where agrivoltaics can mitigate crop yield penalties (even boosting yield) and improve overall profitability," writeresearchers in a journal article for Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).  

A dual-income stream can also offer farmers some insurance should temperature or weather knock out a season's plantings.

"Being able to have that alternate form of income, it's massive for folks who are depending on weather to make their living that is becoming increasingly more extreme and varied," Kinzer said.

Not every farm benefits

So why has adoption been so slow?

"In theory, it's a win-win scenario," Bernacchi said. "But of course, with any technologies, there are always caveats and issues."

One reason is that agrivoltaics don't work everywhere. In America's arid West, where heat stress and less available water can threaten crops, yields stayed the same or even rose under panels. In the humid Midwest, on the other hand, panel shading limited photosynthesis and led to reduced yields in maize and soybeans.  

For cash crops, where there's a very small margin for profit, even a minor reduction in yield is a no-go for many farmers.

Then there's the expense. For solar producers, every added inch to mount panels higher means more labor and steel costs. And farmers might need to find new equipment or change methods to adapt to a new system.

"Farmers want to learn from other farmers," said Kinzer, who works with farmers across the US to see how agrivoltaics are being adopted. "They want to hear from folks who are doing it. And so there's a little bit of a chicken-and-the-egg problem for farmers: In most cases, they can't just go across the street or into the next county over and see a project like this and talk to the farmers doing it."

Bridging the divide between farmers and solar

Solar power's land footprint has made it controversial in certain communities — some farming associations have protested converting farmland into acres of solar panels, arguing their members cease to be farmers and become energy producers instead.

It's a tension agrivoltaics helps to address. 

One survey found that more than 80% of Americans would be more likely to support solar development in their community, if it allowed for the co-production of energy and agriculture — about 10% more than those that support solar development in general. 

"There's this cultural conflict between the farmers who want to farm and the solar companies that want to produce electricity," Bernacchi said. "And agrivoltaics really does bill itself as sort of a middle ground. You can still farm and still get the electricity from the same land."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: India news: Elections 'rigged,' allege Rahul Gandhi and Cockroach party
entries.summary: The Cockroach party has urged India's opposition parties to stop contesting what it calls "rigged" elections and threatened nationwide protests over the Election Commission's voter-list revision. DW has more.
entries.content:
India

India's elections 'rigged,' claim Gandhi and Cockroach party

Published September 25, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

The Cockroach party has urged India's opposition parties to stop contesting what it calls "rigged" elections and threatened nationwide protests over the Election Commission's voter-list revision. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Both the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and the Cockroach Party political movement have labelled India’s elections "rigged"
  • Uproar over the Election Commission of India's (ECI) handling of the voter-list revision remains in spotlight
  • Gandhi and the CJP have claimed voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP
  • Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few

Here are some of the major headlines from India on Friday, September 25:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Another incident of harassment of minor girl surfaces in Bihar

Another incident of harassment of minor girl surfaces in Bihar

Yet another incident where a minor girl was harassed in public in Bihar has surfaced.

A social media video allegedly showed a minor girl being harassed at the Mandar Parvat tourist site in Banka in the eastern state.

Authorities said on Friday they have lodged a case against six unidentified youths after a video emerged that appears to show several young men attacking the girl. Police suspect the footage may be around six months old.

Police are investigating when the incident occurred and trying to identify those seen in the video.

The case comes days after a separate video allegedly showing a minor girl along with her male friend being harassed in Samastipur in Bihar led to the arrest of four people.

Skip next section Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few

Election body's app introduces 'Mark VIP' feature for select few

The Election Commission of India (ECI) introduced a "Mark VIP" feature in an app used by local election officials during the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists, the Hindustan Times newspaper reported.

VIP denotes a Very Important Person.

The feature was added to the BLO App on July 30, according to officials in Delhi's chief electoral officer's office, the newspaper reported. Apple's App Store records described the update as "mark VIP elector related changes."

The ECI did not respond to questions about the feature or the legal basis for its introduction, the report said.

A separate investigation by The Reporters' Collective found that election officials had been instructed to mark ministers, judges, bureaucrats, celebrities and other prominent figures as VIPs during the revision. It reported that such voters could receive preferential treatment, including avoiding hearings required of ordinary voters.

In recent days, Delhi's chief electoral officer has issued notices to nearly 3.3 million voters during the SIR exercise, which included Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal and Foreign Minister S Jaishankar.

Skip next section Cockroach party urges opposition to boycott India's 'rigged' elections

Cockroach party urges opposition to boycott India's 'rigged' elections

Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke on Friday called on India's opposition parties to stop participating in India's "rigged" elections, as it threatened to launch protests across the country on October 2.

"For opposition: Yes, elections are being rigged," Dipke posted on social media, arguing that if the opposition continues to contest such elections, it legitimizes them and "maintain the illusion that they are free and fair."

"If elections are being rigged, it should matter regardless of the state or which party is affected," Dipke wrote, calling on opposition parties to prioritize democracy over political survival. "You cannot keep saying the game is rigged while continuing to play it. Your participation is the only thing that gives these rigged elections legitimacy."

On Thursday, the CJP accused India's Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of undermining the country's democracy and demanded his resignation within 48 hours.

CJP alleged that the Election Commission's voter-roll revision is being used to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

The CJP's demands include:

  • Criminal proceedings against Kumar
  • All upcoming elections put on hold, freeze Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
  • Repeal the 2023 law on the appointment of the Election Commissioners of India

Meanwhile, two petitions were filed in the Bombay High Court on Thursday challenging the SIR process in Maharashtra.

Skip next section Rahul Gandhi accuses Modi, Shah of being behind election 'rigging'

Rahul Gandhi accuses Modi, Shah of being behind election 'rigging'

Both the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and the Cockroach Party political movement called India’s elections "rigged," as the uproar over the Election Commission of India's (ECI) handling of the voter-list revision shows no sign of abating.

On Thursday, Congress Party leader Gandhi alleged that elections in India were being "rigged," and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. It followed a report by Indian Express on objections raised by two election commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists.

The report said that Kumar's fellow Election Commissioners had raised at least 14 objections over 10 months to decisions on voter registrations and electoral data. In one instance, one of the complaints said the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The three commissioners are overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which the ECI says aims to remove deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Critics say the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters, which has benefitted the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"If the vote has been destroyed, then our Constitution has been destroyed. It no longer has power," Gandhi said during a press conference.

Gandhi also alleged that Kumar was elevated to Election Commission head by Prime Minster Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, despite his opposition to the appointment. He went on to accuse them of being "at the top of the conspiracy," and called for them to be investigated.

Meanwhile, BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi defended the ECI, saying on Thursday that the SIR process was legally sound and that the commission’s decisions were based on majority consensus. He said the law empowers the ECI to conduct an SIR at its discretion.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello!

This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the latest updates from across India.

The furor over the Indian Express investigation that thrust the Election Commission of India (ECI) into the spotlight over its handling of the voter-list revision shows no sign of dying down. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and satirical political movement, the Cockroach Party, have both described India's elections as "rigged." The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), however, has rallied in support of the ECI.

Staying with the ECI, it turns out there are citizens who are more equal than others, as the voter-list revision now sees some names marked VIP — Very Important Person. The list is said to include elected representatives, judges, holders of constitutional or other declared offices, and prominent figures from the arts and culture.

Meanwhile, another day and another case of alleged sexual assault in public, a video has surfaced purportedly showing a minor girl being harassed in Bihar again.

For all this and more, follow our live blog!

entries.title: Germany news: Parliament to vote on fuel tax cut
entries.summary: German lawmakers hope to drive down fuel prices by cutting taxes on gas and diesel from October 1. Meanwhile, students in many cities are set to protest against military conscription. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Parliament to vote on fuel tax cut

Published September 25, 2026last updated September 25, 2026

German lawmakers hope to drive down fuel prices by cutting taxes on gas and diesel from October 1. Meanwhile, students in many cities are set to protest against military conscription. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • A fuel tax cut expected to pass Bundestag today as Germany faces high gas prices
  • A state minister reportedly pushes plan to limit asylum right
  • Students across Germany go on strike against potential return of military conscription

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section Condor airline: UK investor Attestor to buy out German state share

Condor airline: UK investor Attestor to buy out German state share

Condor, one of Germany's biggest airlines, will be fully owned by UK investor Attestor by the end of August next year.

The German federal government and the Hesse state government currently own nearly half of the company. The state authorities acquired their stake in 2021, after stepping in to help the carrier as it reeled from the pandemic-related travel disruptions and the 2019 bankruptcy of its UK parent company Thomas Cook.

The airline received state support totaling €930 million ($1.06 billion at the current exchange rate), which it fully paid off by March this year.

Skip next section Rhine levels near Koblenz on record low

Rhine levels near Koblenz on record low

Even with the summer officially over in Germany, the Rhine River, one of the country's essential trade routes, continues to dry up.

The latest data indicate that a gauge at Kaub, near the city of Koblenz, showed only 2 centimeters (less than an inch) of water on Thursday. This would make it the lowest value ever recorded since the measurement began in 1856.

By Friday, it had somewhat recovered to reach 5 centimeters.

It is important to note that these values show the water depth only at the gauge point, which is located relatively close to the shore. The actual navigable depth at Kaub is around 113 centimeters deeper than what's shown at the measuring point.

However, German shipping associations use the gauge value as a reference. Previously, the German Inland Waterways Association (BDB) stated that the Rhine is no longer fully navigable if the gauge values drop into single digits.

Any interruption of Rhine commercial traffic carries major economic risks for Germany. Many businesses use the river as a shipping lane connecting them to large North Sea harbors. In 2023, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy calculated that for every 30 days of low water on the Rhine, Germany's industrial production declines by about 1%.

Skip next section Saxony's interior minister questions Germany's asylum right

Saxony's interior minister questions Germany's asylum right

A four-point plan by conservative Saxon state Interior Minister Armin Schuster aims to limit the right to asylum by changing the European Convention on Human Rights and likely the German constitution, known as the Basic Law, according to multiple media reports.

The minister's plan, seen by the DPA news agency and Redaktionsnetzwerk Deutschland, says the German cities' and municipalities' ability to cope with asylum-seekers should determine how many are allowed in the country, rather than the current law that grants the right to asylum to anyone persecuted on political grounds.

Schuster's initiative would also see rejected asylum-seekers taken into custody in order to ensure deportation.

Germany's laws would be amended to allow a "deportation mandate."

"In order to fully implement the shift in migration policy, we need to ensure deportation for people who are ordered to leave, including criminals and those who do not integrate," Schuster said.

Skip next section Students to protest against potential return of military conscription

Students to protest against potential return of military conscription

Over 100 protests are expected across Germany as students push back on what they believe to be government's efforts to reintroduce military conscription.

The idea has been floated by senior politicians, including a former defense minister and the current premier of Bavaria earlier this month.

Germany has seen several waves of protests against the idea in recent years.

The immediate trigger for the school strike on Friday, however, is the military testing drive for young men in the northern state of Schleswig-Holstein. According to protest organizers, authorities are calling for men born in 2008 to be tested even if they have previously declared no interest in serving in the military.

A spokeswoman for the German Defense Ministry confirmed that the examination is mandatory regardless of the teenagers' stated preferences, though the policy has not yet been implemented all over the country.

Germany suspended mandatory military conscription in 2011.

Skip next section German parliament expected to approve fuel tax cut

German parliament expected to approve fuel tax cut

With oil prices still high on global markets, the German government is cutting the tax on gas and diesel at the gas station, with the move expected to pass the federal parliament later on Friday.

In order to save time, the government has attached the legal changes to a different law. If the measure is passed, it will save German drivers up to 16.7 euro cents per liter (about $0.72 per US gallon) from October 1.

The ADAC motoring association reported that average gas prices in Germany hit a record high last week, reaching €2.308 for a liter of super E10 unleaded and €2.471 for a liter of diesel ($9.98/US gallon and $10.69/US gallon, respectively).

Gas stations are not obligated to pass the full savings to the customers. However, a similar tax cut introduced earlier this year showed a strong effect on gas prices in May and June.

The measure is expected to stay in effect until the end of the year.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

A schönen guten Morgen from DW's news team in Bonn! It is indeed a beautiful, sunny morning in Germany, and good news may be coming — at least for drivers looking to save money at the gas station.

Later today, the country's parliament will vote on a tax cut that should save customers up to 16.7 euro cents per liter (about $0.72 per US gallon), due to go into effect on October 1.

In more somber news, many schools across the country are expected to protest against what they see as the government's push to bring back military conscription.

We will be bringing you updates on these and other top news stories from Germany throughout the day.

entries.title: Italy to ban burqa in schools, limit foreign pupils
entries.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has passed new school rules capping the number of students who don't speak fluent Italian and banning face coverings.
entries.content:
Italy

Italy to ban burqa in schools, limit foreign pupils

September 25, 2026

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has passed new school rules capping the number of students who don't speak fluent Italian and banning face coverings.

Italy's conservative government on Thursday approved a new decree banning face-covering Islamic veils —  including burqas and niqabs —  in schools and putting a limit on the number of students with a poor command of the Italian language in each classroom.

Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, called her Cabinet's measures "tools of common sense that do not divide," adding that they will help integration by avoiding what the right-wing leader called "ghetto classes."

She went on to say the rules would lead to all students receiving the "same opportunities."

Opposition parties and other critics have denounced the move by Meloni's government, with some calling it a "witch hunt” and others accusing the government of turning immigration into more of a political issue ahead of next year's general election.

What do Italy's new school rules entail?

The measures take effect right away but still require parliamentary approval within 60 days. Meloni's coalition currently holds a majority in the country's legislature.

Here is what the decree includes:

  • A per-classroom cap of 30% for foreign students who lack sufficient proficiency in Italian
  • In primary schools, the limit applies to pupils without Italian citizenship who were not born in Italy or did not attend at least two years of preschool
  • In lower and upper secondary schools, the same limit applies to students without Italian citizenship who have not attended the country's school system for at least three years
  • Failure to comply with the decree is punishable by a fine of up to €1,000 euros ($1,140)

Face-coverings banned in schools

The decree bans burqas and niqabs in schools but will continue to allow hijabs.

Meloni said the burqa ban was "a matter of security."

"When a woman — or worse, a young girl — is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," Meloni was quoted as saying in a television interview.

Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the decree would affect about 1,000 classrooms, which come up to 0.3% of the nationwide tally.

According to official data, pupils without Italian citizenship comprised 11.2% of Italy's school population from 2022 to 2023, while classes with over 30% foreign students stood at 7.6% of the total.

What do critics say?

Opponents of the decree are worried that the new measure could force students to attend schools far from the neighborhoods where they live.

Reports have also highlighted concerns among school authorities regarding how the rules would work in areas with large migrant populations.

Independent child rights organization Save the Children had on Wednesday called on the Italian government to weigh the measure "with the utmost political responsibility,” adding that it risked creating discriminatory effects.

"Such a criterion would create ‘first-class' and 'second-class' students," the organization said in its statement.

Meanwhile, opposition leader Elly Schlein railed against the decree, accusing Meloni's government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children."

Meloni is at the head of the most right-wing government that Italy has seen since World War II.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Ethiopia: Internet disrupted in Tigray amid conflict escalation
entries.summary: A web monitor reported an internet disruption in northern Ethiopia amid renewed fighting between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Ethiopia: Internet disrupted in Tigray amid conflict

September 25, 2026

A web monitor reported an internet disruption in northern Ethiopia amid renewed fighting between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government.

Access to the internet has been disrupted in northern Ethiopia's Tigray region, the web monitor NetBlocks reported on Friday.

The region has been the site of renewed hostilities this week that shattered a 2022 peace deal between Ethiopia and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) militia.

During the 2020-2022 Tigray war, the region was largely cut off from the outside world and hundreds of thousands of people were left in famine-like conditions.

"Confirmed: Network data indicate a subnational disruption in ⁠northern ⁠Ethiopia corresponding to reports of a telecoms blackout in Tigray," NetBlocks said.

The cause of the disruption was not immediately clear.

The Reuters news agency cited Tigray residents saying panic buying left shop shelves empty.

"There is deep fear that banks, telecom networks, electricity and basic goods could be cut off again," a local resident told the AFP news agency, adding that there was "panic in the community."

TPLF offensive sparks fear of return to war

The TPLF took control of regional airports in Tigray earlier this week and also clashed with government forces in the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. The militia said it was now in "full-blown war" with Addis Ababa.

The group also formed an anti-government alliance with the Fano militia in Amhara and five other armed groups.

In the 2022-2023 war, Fano fought alongside the federal government against the Tigrayan rebels.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 and was later sidelined alongside the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: How renewed fighting in Tigray could spread across the Horn of Africa
entries.summary: The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

How Tigray's renewed fighting could spread in Horn of Africa

September 25, 2026

The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.

Fighting has erupted again in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive on September 23, with fighting also reported in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara. 

The escalation threatens the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war between Ethiopia's federal government in Addis Ababa and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

But the central question is bigger than the return of war to Tigray: could the conflict connect with the wars and rivalries already destabilizing the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?

Martin Plaut, a British journalist and Horn of Africa expert, argues the conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders.

"If a conflict were to spill over, it is quite possible that a conflict involving Eritrea and Ethiopia could then involve Sudanese forces as well, which could drag the whole region into a war," he told DW in an exclusive interview.

Jalale Getachew Birru, a senior analyst for East Africa at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also stressed that the conflict cannot be viewed in isolation. ACLED is an independent conflict-monitoring and research organization that collects and analyzes data on political violence and armed conflict around the world.

“The Ethiopia[n] case is not [an] isolated case for the Horn of Africa. It involves the neighboring countries as well, and it's being displayed across the Horn of Africa countries," Birru told DW.

Her assessment points to a broader regional dynamic: Ethiopia's conflict is unfolding alongside shifting alliances and competing interests in neighboring Sudan and Somalia. ACLED's current analysis likewise places the renewed Tigray conflict within a wider pattern of instability across the Horn of Africa.

The risk is not based on a single regional alliance. It comes from the fact that several conflicts are already geographically and politically connected, Birru noted.

African Union urges restraint

The African Union (AU) has also expressed deep concern about the possibility of further destabilization.

In a statement on September 23, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf warned that new political and military alliances risk reversing the progress made since 2020.

The AU called for an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions, renewed direct talks under the Pretoria agreement and restraint by Ethiopia's neighbors. It also tasked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's high representative for the Horn of Africa, with supporting diplomatic efforts.

The AU's intervention reflects concerns that the crisis could have wider regional implications, including the possibility that it could interact with conflicts beyond Ethiopia's borders.

Old enemies, new alliances

The TPLF recently joined six other Ethiopian armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Among them is the Amhara Fano movement, which fought against the TPLF during the previous war.

The alliance is not a unified military force, and its members have different political objectives and territorial interests. But its formation could leave the Ethiopian government facing several fronts at once.

The fighting in Afar, a northeastern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Djibouti, is particularly significant. The region contains the main transport corridor linking landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti, through which much of Ethiopia's international trade passes. Sustained fighting there could therefore threaten a vital economic lifeline.

And beyond Afar lies Eritrea.

Eritrea's potential role

During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Since then, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, Eritrea's capital, have deteriorated. Ethiopia's ambitions for access to the Red Sea have added to Eritrea's security concerns.

"The war could certainly escalate, and Eritrea could become involved," Plaut said.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups opposed to the government, while Asmara has denied such allegations. The extent of any direct Eritrean involvement remains difficult to establish independently.

Sudan: Where conflicts could collide

Sudan has been at war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has drawn in regional powers and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.

Plaut argues that Ethiopia and Eritrea are already indirectly involved on opposing sides.

"The Ethiopians are on the side of the RSF and Hemedti," he said, referring to its commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. "There has been strong evidence that there is a base in western Ethiopia which is supplying and training RSF fighters," Plaut added. DW has not independently verified that claim.

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has faced allegations of supporting the RSF, which it denies. Plaut identifies Eritrea, Egypt and Saudi Arabia as supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces.

"So both Eritrea and Ethiopia are already playing a role, indirectly, in the war," he said.

If Ethiopia and Eritrea were to enter direct hostilities, Sudan's rival forces could have incentives to exploit the new situation, Plaut said. Fighting could put additional pressure on Sudan's eastern frontier and alter supply routes and military calculations.

Plaut sees the danger of a chain reaction: "Because you have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces, this could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."

"So the whole thing becomes a generalized conflict in the region," he said.

Red Sea connection

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping choke points, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

Eritrea and Djibouti lie on its western side, Yemen on the eastern side. The war in Yemen has already shown how insecurity around the Red Sea can disrupt international shipping and draw in outside powers.

Eritrea's location and its control of the port of Assab give it strategic importance far beyond Tigray. Any major deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations could therefore affect the wider security architecture of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also developed extensive political, economic and security interests across the Horn of Africa. Their interests overlap in some areas but diverge in others, particularly over Sudan.

Danger is escalation, not inevitability

None of this means that a regional war is inevitable. There is no evidence of a single military alliance stretching from Tigray to the Gulf. Ethiopia's armed groups have competing interests, Eritrea may avoid direct intervention, and Sudan's warring parties have their own priorities.

But conflicts do not need a common command structure to become interconnected.

The Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. The Pretoria agreement stopped the large-scale fighting, but many of the political and territorial disputes underlying the conflict remained unresolved.

Today, Tigray is again at war while Ethiopia faces several armed movements, Eritrea is a potential military actor, and Sudan is already engulfed in civil war.

Plaut warns that the humanitarian consequences could again be severe.

"There's certainly a danger of this becoming an extremely bloody conflict," he told DW. "After all, 600,000 people died in the last one in Tigray."

But he does not predict that the previous death toll will necessarily be exceeded. "Let's hope that it doesn't go in that direction," he said.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
entries.summary: Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods a "warning to the world" — and questioned if the world had "really heard that warning."
entries.content:
September 25, 2026

Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods a "warning to the world" — and questioned if the world had "really heard that warning."

Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's prime minister stood at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in his UNGA address Thursday.

Nepal's leader calls for cooperation to protect the Himalayas

The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas. 

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster. 

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

Nepal paying 'colossal' price for climate change

Shah noted that his country contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he was not blaming any individual nation or continent.

"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.

Grants, not loans, necessary for flood recovery

The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of responsibility, reparation and resilience as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.

Shah said vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

The 36-year-old Shah was the youngest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.

Nepal-Tibet floods — the deadly 'Himalayan tsunami'

On August 26, a glacier collapsed near the border between Nepal and China's ​Tibet Autonomous Region, unleashing landslides and a flash flood that ripped through downstream valleys.

In the days after the disaster, the world watched powerful images of the widespread destruction emerge from Nepal.

Entire villages were flattened. In other visuals, people trapped in hydropower tunnels deep within the Himalayas were seen crawling away a thick sludge of mud to reach rescuers.

Over 6,000 people are still reported to be missing, with search and recovery efforts still ongoing.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar and Sean Sinico

entries.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
entries.summary: A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.
